note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FOLLOW THE STEM
tiles.details: Trace a living flowering stem to its fibrous-rooted base and check whether lower nodes really produce adventitious roots. Both currently public same-species photographs (panels 1–2) are general plant references, NOT proof of a connected rooted node. Do not draw a rooting-node arrow on either.
tiles.short: Creeping/ascending ANNUAL; look for actual roots at lower nodes.

tiles.heading: 02 · TRACE THE FLOWERING RACEMES
tiles.details: Published accounts describe 5–15 short one-sided racemes about 1–4 cm long, with crowded paired spikelets; some regional descriptions give 3–6(–12) racemes. The two publicly eligible U. reptans panels are general source-labelled plants, not verified measured branch/spikelet anatomy. The better archived CC BY-NC reproductive macros are retained for evidence but are NOT in the public gallery; do not reference their former panel positions.
tiles.short: Usually 5–15 one-sided racemes, about 1–4 cm long.
tiles.status: FIELD HEAD CUE — NO PUBLIC MEASURED RACEME/SPIKELET PHOTO

tiles.heading: 03 · TRUE COLLAR, NOT SHEATH HAIRS
tiles.details: The true ligule is a short hair fringe (regional treatment ~1 mm). Open the inner blade–sheath junction on the same plant and photograph it at 10–20× with a 1-mm scale. No current public U. reptans panel resolves this structure, so this tile intentionally has no photo reference or ligule arrow.
tiles.short: Ligule is a short ~1 mm HAIR FRINGE.

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE A RIPE SPIKELET
tiles.details:
Supplemental field cue (Flora of North America, Urochloa reptans) — Use a scale to measure one whole spikelet. The treatment gives 1.8–2.2 mm and describes most spikelets as paired and held close to the branch.

Measure 5–10 mature U. reptans spikelets beside a 1-mm ruler (Kew about 1.5–2.2 mm; regional treatments to ~2.5 mm). Separate the tiny truncate/cufflike lower glume (~0.4–0.6 mm, 1/8–1/4 total length), nearly spikelet-length upper glume (~1.7–2.2 mm; about 5–9 veins depending on treatment), and lower sterile lemma. The genuine archived reproductive macros are CC BY-NC and withheld from the public gallery; neither current open-license subject panel proves a measured glume.
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — NO PUBLIC SCALED TARGET-SPECIES GLUME

tiles.heading: 05 · FIND THE FLORETS AND AWN ORIGIN
tiles.details: Dissect a ripe spikelet to show the lower sterile/staminate floret (membranous five-veined lemma and palea) and the upper hard, transversely wrinkled fertile lemma (roughly 1–2 mm, inrolled margins). The tiny terminal mucro is NOT a long projecting awn. No current public U. reptans image proves these structures, so do not link a look-alike photo or place speculative arrows.
tiles.short: Lower sterile/male floret + upper HARD wrinkled fertile lemma.

tiles.heading: 06 · COMPARE AND RELEASE GATE
tiles.details: Current public gallery panels 3–6 (zero-based indices 2–5) are ALL different-species comparisons: U. fusca reproductive and vegetative images and U. texana habit/panicle. Published ripe-spikelet ranges: U. reptans ~1.5–2.2 mm with lower glume ~1/8–1/4; U. fusca ~2.4–3.4 mm with lower glume often ~1/4–1/3; U. texana ~4.5–5.9 mm with lower glume ~1/2–2/3. No same-scale comparison is currently verified. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: actual rooted nodes, measured true hair-fringe ligule, scaled ripe paired spikelets and dissected glumes/lemmas with public rights. NEEDS_SITE_QA: confirm all six current panels, four different-species labels, original arrow endpoints, rights filtering and mobile render. Remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Smaller spikelets than U. fusca and U. texana; not FINISHED.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: CREEPING SIGNALGRASS: source-labelled photo shows multiple slender radiating racemes with tiny crowded spikelets. Verify 1.5–2.2 mm ripe spikelets and their extremely short lower glume (about 1/8–1/4). In vegetative material, seek real lower STEM NODES rooting on the soil—do not infer rooted creeping stems from an isolated seedhead photograph.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST TWO PUBLIC PHOTOS: the Dan Johnson CC BY 4.0 and 葉子 CC0 records are species-labelled living Urochloa reptans. Use them for general taxon context only; their true ligules, individual glumes and rooted nodes are not pixel-certified.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The true ligule is a short hair fringe (regional treatment ~1 mm). Open the inner blade–sheath junction on the same plant and photograph it at 10–20× with a 1-mm scale. No current public U. reptans panel resolves this structure, so this tile intentionally has no photo reference or ligule arrow.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Published accounts describe 5–15 short one-sided racemes about 1–4 cm long, with crowded paired spikelets; some regional descriptions give 3–6(–12) racemes. The two publicly eligible U. reptans panels are general source-labelled plants, not verified measured branch/spikelet anatomy. The better archived CC BY-NC reproductive macros are retained for evidence but are NOT in the public gallery; do not reference their former panel positions.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Despite the photo's spread-out branches, published U. reptans descriptions report 5–15 often closely spaced racemes with crowded PAIRED spikelets along each branch; a 'loose head' alone is misleading. U. fusca has typically larger plumper ~2.4–3.4 mm spikelets, lower glume ~1/4–1/3, and U. texana much larger 4.5–5.9 mm units with lower glume reaching roughly half to two-thirds.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: CREEPING SIGNALGRASS: source-labelled photo shows multiple slender radiating racemes with tiny crowded spikelets. Verify 1.5–2.2 mm ripe spikelets and their extremely short lower glume (about 1/8–1/4). In vegetative material, seek real lower STEM NODES rooting on the soil—do not infer rooted creeping stems from an isolated seedhead photograph.
memory_rule: U. reptans tiny ~1.5–2.2 mm and minute basal glume; U. fusca blunt ~2.4–3.4 mm with shorter glume; U. texana much larger ~4.5–5.9 mm with lower glume about half/two-thirds.
safety_note: Strict site display filter removes five CC BY-NC teaching panels (four same species, one U. fusca comparison). Six publicly eligible panels remain, of which only two represent U. reptans. No true ligule, glume dissection or rooted node photographed at diagnostic quality. Scientific photo gaps and Pages render QA remain.
field_rule: Rank photos by what they truly show: flowering branch/shape first, followed by mature spikelet length and lower glume measured under 10–20×. Do not treat unmeasured photogenic heads as proof of native versus introduced species.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Despite the photo's spread-out branches, published U. reptans descriptions report 5–15 often closely spaced racemes with crowded PAIRED spikelets along each branch; a 'loose head' alone is misleading. U. fusca has typically larger plumper ~2.4–3.4 mm spikelets, lower glume ~1/4–1/3, and U. texana much larger 4.5–5.9 mm units with lower glume reaching roughly half to two-thirds.
